evals.prompt: We are launching a public fintech web application in ap-south-1 with a React SPA on S3 and an ALB-backed API in a VPC. Design our Well-Architected Edge & DDoS Perimeter (`SEC05`, `SEC06`) covering S3 + ALB origin locking via CloudFront, security response headers, WAFv2 rule tuning, L3/L4/L7 DDoS protection, and outbound domain exfiltration filtering inside the VPC.
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-well-architected-security-compliance and designs: CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) for both S3 (with all 4 BlockPublicAccess flags + SecureTransport deny) and VPC/ALB origins, managed SecurityHeadersPolicy (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options), AWS WAFv2 with rate-based rules (>=100 req/5min) and AWS Managed Rules deployed in Count mode first before Block, AWS Shield Advanced with automatic L7 mitigation, and Route 53 DNS Firewall for outbound VPC domain filtering.
expectations: Activates the aws-well-architected-security-compliance skill and maintains strictly read-only behavior
Specifies Amazon CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC) for S3/VPC/ALB origins (replacing legacy OAI and public S3 buckets) plus managed SecurityHeadersPolicy (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options)

Specifies AWS WAFv2 rate-based rules and deploying AWS Managed Rule Groups in Count mode first to tune false positives before switching to Block, paired with AWS Shield Advanced for L3/L4/L7 DDoS protection
Includes Amazon Route 53 DNS Firewall associated with the VPC to filter outbound malicious/exfiltration DNS domains

evals.prompt: Our data team has an S3 bucket storing 500 million small parquet objects encrypted with SSE-KMS using a Customer Managed Key, and their monthly KMS API bill spiked to thousands of dollars—plus their CloudFormation template lacks TLS transport enforcement and KMS key rotation. Write a Security Pillar (`SEC08`, `SEC09`) compliant CloudFormation template for the KMS CMK and S3 bucket that cuts KMS request costs by up to 99%, enforces TLS-only access and public access blocks, and validate it with your IaC compliance tools.
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-well-architected-security-compliance, authors a CloudFormation template with AWS::KMS::Key (EnableKeyRotation: true, scoped KeyPolicy) and AWS::S3::Bucket (BucketKeyEnabled: true reducing KMS GenerateDataKey/Decrypt calls by up to 99%, all 4 PublicAccessBlockConfiguration flags true, VersioningConfiguration Enabled, DeletionPolicy: Retain) + AWS::S3::BucketPolicy denying aws:SecureTransport: false, and validates it with aws-iac validate_cloudformation_template and check_cloudformation_template_compliance.
expectations: Activates the aws-well-architected-security-compliance skill and runs aws-iac MCP validation tools (validate_cloudformation_template and check_cloudformation_template_compliance) without running raw shell CLI commands
Configures BucketKeyEnabled: true on the S3 SSE-KMS configuration and explains how S3 Bucket Keys generate bucket-level data keys to reduce KMS API request costs by up to 99%
Enforces EnableKeyRotation: true on the KMS CMK, all four PublicAccessBlockConfiguration flags set to true, and an S3 BucketPolicy explicitly denying requests where aws:SecureTransport is false

evals.prompt: Audit this proposed EKS/ECS workload configuration against the Well-Architected Compute & Container Hardening baseline (`SEC06`): images pushed to ECR with mutable `:latest` tags and `ScanOnPush: false`, containers running as `uid: 0` with a writable root filesystem, and EC2 worker nodes launched from unverified community AMIs with SSH port 22 open and IMDSv1 enabled. Provide the complete hardened platform specification.
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-well-architected-security-compliance and remediates every gap: Golden AMIs/images via EC2 Image Builder + Amazon Inspector continuous scanning, ECR ImageTagMutability: IMMUTABLE + ScanOnPush: true, container non-root UID + readonlyRootFilesystem: true + drop ALL capabilities, IMDSv2 (HttpTokens: required, HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 2 for container hosts), and SSM Session Manager with zero port 22/3389 ingress.
expectations: Activates the aws-well-architected-security-compliance skill
Mandates ECR ImageTagMutability: IMMUTABLE and ScanOnPush: true (with Amazon Inspector scanning) plus building hardened Golden AMIs via EC2 Image Builder rather than unverified community AMIs
Enforces non-root container execution, readonlyRootFilesystem: true, IMDSv2 (HttpTokens: required, HttpPutResponseHopLimit: 2 for container hosts), and AWS SSM Session Manager instead of SSH port 22

evals.prompt: When we run proactive CloudFormation compliance checks (`cfn-guard`) on an internet-facing Application Load Balancer Security Group that intentionally allows `0.0.0.0/0` inbound on TCP `443` for customer HTTPS traffic, a strict CIDR rule flags `0.0.0.0/0`. How should our platform team structure the ALB + backend tier Security Groups, TLS policy, WAFv2 compensating control, and template compliance documentation without weakening private-tier rules?
evals.expected_output: Activates aws-well-architected-security-compliance, distinguishes public ingress on ALB TCP 443 (allowed ONLY with TLS 1.2/1.3 policy ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-2021-06 + AWS WAFv2 WebACL attached + HTTP 80 redirecting to 443, documented explicitly in template metadata/suppression) from backend ECS/EC2/RDS Security Groups (which MUST remain in private/isolated subnets and reference only the upstream ALB/App Security Group ID—never 0.0.0.0/0 or broad CIDRs).
expectations: Activates the aws-well-architected-security-compliance skill

Requires mandatory compensating controls on the public ALB TCP 443 exception: TLS 1.2/1.3 minimum security policy, attached AWS WAFv2 WebACL, and explicit documentation/granular metadata suppression rather than disabling compliance checks globally

Enforces strict source-Security-Group chaining (referencing the ALB Security Group ID on the private compute SG, and compute SG ID on the isolated database SG) with zero 0.0.0.0/0 ingress on backend compute or databases

evals.prompt: Our security audit (`SEC05`) found that workloads in private subnets call S3, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager, and KMS over public internet NAT Gateways, and an engineer asks whether simply creating VPC Endpoints is enough to stop data exfiltration to an attacker's external AWS account S3 bucket from inside the VPC. evals.expected_output: Activates aws-well-architected-security-compliance, explains provisioning Gateway Endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) and Interface Endpoints (Secrets Manager, KMS, ECR, Logs) with scoped Security Groups, and clarifies that default VPC Endpoint policies (`"*"`) still allow authenticated calls to an external attacker's S3 bucket over PrivateLink—requiring scoped VPC Endpoint Policies (`aws:PrincipalOrgID` and `aws:ResourceOrgID`) + S3 BlockPublicAccess / RCPs.
expectations: Activates the aws-well-architected-security-compliance skill
Explains why default unrestricted VPC Endpoint policies still permit an attacker with stolen credentials inside the VPC to write data to an external AWS account's S3 bucket over the VPC Endpoint

Prescribes attaching scoped VPC Endpoint Policies enforcing aws:PrincipalOrgID and aws:ResourceOrgID (data perimeter) alongside private/isolated subnet segmentation and Interface Endpoint Security Groups

evals.prompt: Our enterprise connects two data centers to AWS in ap-south-1—one via AWS Site-to-Site VPN and one via a dedicated 10 Gbps AWS Direct Connect fiber connection—and our compliance officer points out that standard BGP over Direct Connect VLANs is unencrypted by default (`SEC09`). expectations: Activates the aws-well-architected-security-compliance skill
Confirms that native AWS Direct Connect traffic is not encrypted by default and requires explicit transit encryption to satisfy SEC09

Contrasts Direct Connect MACsec (Layer-2 IEEE 802.1AE hop-by-hop line-rate encryption on supported 10G/100G dedicated connections) against IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect (Layer-3 end-to-end tunnel encryption with ECMP scaling) plus end-to-end TLS 1.2/1.3
